title: What Does the Encoder Actually Decide? A Controlled Comparison of 64 Vision Backbones on Joint Tree Segmentation and Stereo Depth

paper.title:
What Does the Encoder Actually Decide? A Controlled Comparison of
64 Vision Backbones on Joint Tree Segmentation and Stereo Depth
paper.abstract:
Abstract A robot that prunes trees needs two facts about the same pixel: whether it
belongs to a tree, and how far away it is. Both are normally obtained by
attaching a task head to a vision backbone, and the backbone is chosen by
reputation rather than by measurement. We ask a narrow but answerable
question: with the dataset, the decoders, the losses, the schedule and the
evaluation all held fixed, how much does the choice of encoder actually
change joint semantic segmentation and stereo depth on thin vegetation? We
build a hard parameter-sharing network in which one shared encoder feeds a
segmentation branch and a stereo branch, and in which only the
encoder is swapped — a one-string change that retunes nothing downstream.
We evaluate 64 encoders, one canonical representative per
architecture family across 8 groups (classical, lightweight and
modern CNNs, plain and hierarchical transformers, hybrids, MLP-mixers and
state-space models), each at the preset nearest a common ∼ \sim 25 M budget
and trained from scratch so that a pretrained checkpoint is not the
confound; where a family publishes nothing near that budget, capacity is
analysed explicitly rather than assumed away.
Evaluation is deliberately unforgiving: depth is scored on tree
pixels only, and segmentation is scored with boundary F1 and background IoU
that a “label-everything-tree” collapse cannot win. Three findings stand
out. First, the strongest encoders are convolutional and hybrid, not
transformer: internimage_t leads with 0.650 segmentation mIoU and
0.725 depth δ 1 \delta_{1} , while 3 of the
4 plain vision transformers collapse when trained from scratch.
Second, parameters do not predict quality — edgenext_xxs, at only
1.2 M encoder parameters, outranks models nearly two
orders of magnitude larger. Third,
the segmentation and depth rankings agree strongly (Spearman ρ = 0.89 \rho=0.89{} ), so the shared encoder faces no genuine task conflict
and a single backbone serves both. Along
the way, 25 of 64 encoders collapse to a
degenerate all-tree segmentation that region IoU hides but boundary F1
exposes — a reminder that the metric, not only the backbone, decides what
a comparison can see.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: A robot that prunes trees must answer two questions about the same pixel. The first is one of membership: is this pixel part of a tree, or part of the background behind it? The second is one of geometry: how far away is it? Neither answer is useful alone. Perfect segmentation without depth cannot guide a cutter; perfect depth without a tree mask cannot tell the cutter where the wood is. Both tasks are, in practice, built the same way: take a vision backbone, attach a decoder, and train. The backbone holds most of the parameters and most of the compute, and it is usually chosen by reputation — whatever performed well on ImageNet classification, or whatever the previous paper in the area used. That inheritance is rarely questioned, and it is not obviously safe. Tree canopies are not ImageNet: the objects are thin, self-occluding, repetitive and semi-transparent, and the discriminative signal lives in high-frequency boundaries rather than in object-level texture. This paper asks a deliberately narrow question, because the narrow version is the one that can be answered: with everything else held fixed, how much does the encoder decide? We are not proposing a new architecture. We are measuring how much the architecture choice is worth on a task whose conventional wisdom was formed somewhere else. Answering it requires a setup in which the encoder is genuinely the only thing that changes, and an evaluation that cannot be won by a shortcut: trees fill 75–91% of every tree50 frame, so region IoU is nearly saturated before a model has learned anything. We therefore score depth on tree pixels only and segmentation with boundary F1 and background IoU, which a “label-everything-tree” collapse cannot win. Our contributions are: • A two-task benchmark in which the encoder is the only free variable. A hard parameter-sharing network feeds one shared encoder into a segmentation branch and a stereo branch. Every encoder exposes the same five-scale feature contract, so swapping it is a one-string change; the decoders, losses, schedule and evaluation never move. • 64 encoders, one per family, from scratch. One canonical representative per architecture family across 8 groups, taken at the preset nearest a common budget with ablation-only variants excluded, and trained without pretrained weights so that a checkpoint is not the confound. Where families publish nothing near that budget, capacity is measured rather than assumed away. • An evaluation designed to resist the obvious cheat. Depth on tree pixels only; segmentation reported with boundary F1 and background IoU alongside region IoU, so a degenerate all-tree solution is visible rather than rewarded. • A measured answer. Convolutional and hybrid encoders lead while most plain transformers collapse from scratch; parameter count does not predict quality; and the segmentation and depth orderings are strongly correlated, so one shared backbone suffices for both tasks.

sections.heading: II-A Perception for Tree and Orchard Robotics
sections.text: Robots that work on woody plants — harvesting, thinning, pruning, forwarding — have converged on the same perception requirement: a per-pixel decision about what is plant and where it is in space [ 28 , 29 ] . Field pruning systems report that perception, not manipulation, is the binding constraint [ 30 ] , and the first autonomous forestry machines make the same observation at a larger scale [ 31 ] . What these systems need from a network is exactly the pair we study: a tree mask that follows the true silhouette, and a depth estimate on the pixels inside it. Two properties of the domain make it a poor match for the assumptions behind ImageNet-era backbone design. First, the targets are thin : branches and twigs are a few pixels wide, so the signal lives in high-frequency boundaries rather than object-level texture — the same difficulty that motivated dedicated treatment of wires and cables in aerial robotics [ 32 ] . Second, exact labels on thin structures are effectively unobtainable by hand, which is why rendered data has become a standard instrument for agricultural segmentation [ 33 ] and is what we use here. What is missing from this literature is a controlled measurement of how much the backbone contributes, which is the gap this paper addresses.

sections.heading: II-B Vision Backbones
sections.text: The encoder families we compare correspond to the main lines of backbone research. Classical convolutional networks established depth, residual connections and cardinality as the levers of representational power [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Efficiency-driven designs traded dense convolution for depthwise-separable and shuffled operations to reach mobile budgets [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Vision transformers replaced the inductive bias of convolution with global attention [ 8 , 9 ] , and hierarchical variants reintroduced locality and multi-scale structure to make attention affordable for dense prediction [ 10 , 11 ] . Modern convolutional networks then showed that much of the transformer advantage could be recovered by convolutional designs with large kernels and modernised training recipes [ 12 , 13 ] . Hybrids interleave the two families [ 14 , 15 ] , attention-free MLP designs question whether attention is required at all [ 16 , 17 ] , and state-space models offer linear-complexity sequence mixing as a third alternative [ 18 , 19 ] . These families are usually compared on ImageNet classification, occasionally on COCO detection or ADE20K segmentation. We are not aware of a controlled comparison on a task that couples dense semantic segmentation with stereo geometry on thin structures, which is the regime this paper targets.

sections.heading: II-C Multi-Task Learning
sections.text: Sharing one encoder between related tasks is the standard way to amortise computation, and hard parameter sharing — one shared trunk, independent task-specific heads — remains the reference formulation [ 20 , 21 ] . Richer schemes add cross-task connections, cascades or attention between branches [ 22 , 23 ] . We deliberately use the plain hard-sharing form: any cross-task pathway would give the encoder a second route to influence the result and would blur exactly the attribution this paper is trying to make.

sections.heading: II-D Stereo Matching and Segmentation
sections.text: Our stereo branch follows the cost-volume lineage: features are correlated across a disparity range, aggregated with 3D convolutions, and reduced by soft-argmin [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] . The segmentation branch is a standard U-Net encoder–decoder [ 27 ] that fuses the five encoder scales into a per-pixel tree/background labelling. Both branches are held fixed across all 64 encoders; the only thing that changes between runs is the shared trunk that feeds them.

sections.heading: III-A Data
sections.text: We use the tree50 corpus: 50 rendered forest scenes, each captured from 48 viewpoints, giving 2,400 rectified stereo pairs at 1920 × 1080 1920\times 1080 with per-pixel depth and tree masks. Splits are scene-exclusive — scenes 1–40 train, 41–45 validate, 46–50 test — so no tree is ever seen from a different angle at test time. Because the renderer exports geometry rather than hand annotation, the labels are exact on precisely the thin structures that manual labelling cannot reach. We state the size of the test set in the units that matter: it is 240 frames but only 5 independent scenes , since the 48 views of one scene show the same trees. Everything reported below is therefore an average over 5 trees, and Section VI-D quantifies what that costs in confidence. Two measured properties of the data shaped the design, and each is enforced by an assertion in the codebase rather than left as a convention. First, disparity is an exact function of depth, d = f x ​ B / z d=f_{x}B/z , agreeing with the rendered output to 0.0 0.0 px on average; depth and disparity are therefore the same signal in two units, so the network predicts disparity once and converts. Second, trees occupy 75–91% of the pixels. This is why region IoU is a weak metric here and why depth is scored on tree pixels only (Section IV ).

sections.heading: III-C The Five-Scale Contract
sections.text: The comparison is only meaningful if the encoder is genuinely interchangeable. Every encoder implements one method, forward_features , returning five maps whose i i -th spatial size is exactly ⌈ H / 2 i + 1 ⌉ \lceil H/2^{i+1}\rceil . The contract fixes ratios , not sizes, so the same encoder serves any input resolution; only the channel counts differ. Inputs are reflection-padded to a multiple of 32 and each level is cropped back, so padding never leaks into the feature sizes.

sections.heading: III-D Encoder Selection
sections.text: Two levels of organisation are used throughout and are not interchangeable. A family is one published architecture line (ResNeXt, Swin, ConvNeXt, …); a group is the broad design paradigm it belongs to, of which there are 8, labelled A–I. We select one representative per family , giving 64 encoders spread over the 8 groups. The selection applies three rules, in order. First, exclude ablation-only variants : several families ship control conditions alongside their proposal — a large-kernel network with the kernels reduced to 3 × 3 3\times 3 , a state-space model with the state-space mixing removed — and representing a family by its own control would understate it. Second, target the parameter budget : among the remainder we take the preset closest to a common ∼ \sim 25 M encoder budget, the tier at which most families publish their reference model. Third, prefer canonical naming when the first two rules tie. A small hand-curated override fixes the cases where the automatic rule still picks a non-canonical variant. We state plainly that this targets a budget rather than matching one. Families do not publish on a common grid: only 22 of 64 encoders (34%) land within ± \pm 10 M of the target, the median is 11.7 M, and the range is 0.2–100.3 M — four families whose smallest published variant is a ∼ \sim 100 M base model are represented at that size. Rather than discard the families that do not fit, we keep them and treat capacity as a measured covariate: Fig. 3 plots quality directly against encoder size, and the result — that the largest models are among the worst — is what licenses reading the rest of the comparison as being about architecture rather than about scale.

sections.heading: IV Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: All metrics are computed on the left image of the test split.

sections.heading: IV-A Segmentation
sections.text: We report tree-versus-background mean IoU (mIoU), the individual background and tree IoUs, boundary F1 at a 2 px tolerance (BF1), and pixel accuracy. The metric we consider most diagnostic is not region IoU but boundary F1 together with background IoU . Because trees fill most of the frame, a model that simply labels every pixel “tree” already scores ∼ \sim 0.93 tree IoU while contributing nothing: its background IoU is near zero and its boundary F1 collapses. Region IoU hides this failure; the boundary and background terms expose it. Since the downstream task needs the tree silhouette , the boundary term is the one that matters.

sections.heading: IV-B Depth
sections.text: Depth is evaluated on ground-truth tree pixels only . Sky and ground are geometrically trivial and would dilute the metric with the easy majority. We report AbsRel, RMSE, SILog and δ < 1.25 k \delta<1.25^{k} , plus disparity EPE and bad- τ \tau rates on the same pixel set. One property of this pixel set deserves stating, because it makes the mean error look worse than the prediction is. Tree pixels include distant twigs at the far end of the disparity range, where a sub-pixel disparity error maps to a metric depth error of several metres. The absolute error is therefore strongly right-skewed, and mean-based scores are set by that tail rather than by the typical pixel: the best encoder has 0.786 AbsRel and 1.39 m mean absolute error, but a median absolute error of 0.20 m, with 2.45 m at the 90th percentile. We report the mean-based metrics because they are the convention and keep this work comparable, but read them as tail statistics; the median and the percentiles describe what a controller would see on most of the branch it is actually reaching for. Two secondary views are reported because they answer questions the primary one hides: per-tree averaging weights each tree equally rather than each pixel, so a model that has learned only the large foreground tree separates from one that also handles the distant small ones; and depth restricted to the predicted tree mask measures end-to-end usability, since a segmentation error propagates into the depth that is actually consumed.

sections.heading: IV-C Efficiency
sections.text: We report end-to-end FPS, peak memory, encoder parameters and GFLOPs, measured on the whole two-branch network. Since the decoders are byte-identical across runs, differences between rows are attributable to the encoder even though the figures themselves are whole-system costs.

sections.heading: V Experimental Setup
sections.text: All encoders are trained from scratch — no pretrained weights — so that the comparison measures architecture rather than the availability and quality of a checkpoint. This lowers absolute accuracy and is a deliberate trade; it also means the ranking here need not match one obtained with pretrained initialisation, a point we return to in the limitations. Every encoder receives an identical schedule: AdamW at learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 2 10^{-2} , cosine decay after linear warmup, mixed precision, gradient clipping at norm 1.0 1.0 , and 100 epochs at 512 × 288 512\times 288 with batch size 12. Normalisation layers and biases are excluded from weight decay. The checkpoint is selected by lowest total validation loss rather than by any single task metric, since selecting on one metric would quietly turn the run into single-task model selection. The segmentation branch is supervised by cross-entropy and the stereo branch by smooth- L 1 L_{1} on disparity at both the coarse and refined stages. The cost volume is built at stride 4 over a disparity range that covers the native maximum, and the segmentation decoder uses channel widths ( 128 , 96 , 64 , 48 ) (128,96,64,48) . Every resolution-dependent constant — chiefly the disparity search range and the boundary-F1 tolerance — is defined once at native resolution and derived for any other resolution by a single function, so that supervision and evaluation cannot silently disagree. Encoders are trained in isolated subprocesses so that a memory failure in one cannot corrupt the allocator state of the next. Where an encoder does not fit at the nominal batch size, the micro-batch is reduced and gradient accumulation is raised to hold the effective batch constant; holding the effective batch fixed matters because batch size changes normalisation statistics and gradient noise, and an encoder penalised for a memory property rather than for its representational quality would defeat the purpose of the comparison. State-space and global-attention encoders are the systematic pressure point here, since their activation memory far exceeds what their parameter count suggests; of the full selection, 64 encoders completed training and are reported below.

sections.heading: VI-A Overall Comparison
sections.text: Table I reports all 64 encoders in rank order. The strongest is internimage_t (Modern CNN), which combines 0.650 segmentation mIoU with the best depth of the whole study (0.725 δ 1 \delta_{1} , 10.85 px EPE), for a composite of 0.688. It is followed by a classical wide residual network and a hierarchical transformer, and the top of the ranking is dominated by convolutional and hybrid designs. The best segmentation in isolation belongs to densenet121 (0.654 mIoU, and the highest boundary F1), and the best disparity error to internimage_t; the lowest AbsRel is swin_tiny_w4 at 0.358. No plain vision transformer appears near the top: 3 of the 4 collapse outright, and the exception, deit_tiny_patch16, only reaches rank 23 (Section VI-B ). The comparison also exposes a failure the region metric would have hidden. 25 of 64 encoders collapse to a degenerate solution that labels almost everything “tree”: their tree IoU stays near 0.93 0.93 , yet their background IoU and boundary F1 fall to near zero and their mIoU drops to ∼ \sim 0.46. Region IoU alone would have ranked these models as competent; the boundary and background terms correctly place them at the bottom. This is the concrete payoff of the metric choice in Section IV , and Section VI-F shows what the collapse looks like on the image.

The strongest median group is the CNN-Transformer Hybrids (G, median score 0.600), narrowly ahead of the Modern CNNs; classical CNNs and hierarchical transformers follow. The weakest by a wide margin is the Plain Transformer group (E, 0.329): plain ViTs are data-hungry, and without pretraining 3 of the 4 never acquire the boundaries that segmentation and thin-structure depth depend on. The pattern inside the group is itself informative. The two members that carry ∼ \sim 100 M parameters are the two worst, while the survivor, deit_tiny_patch16, is also the smallest at 6.4 M and reaches rank 23 — so the group’s poor showing is a statement about the training regime, and if anything capacity makes it worse. The more useful observation is about variance . Within-group spread is comparable to between-group spread: the classical-CNN group alone runs from the second-best encoder overall down to nearly the worst. In other words, which encoder matters at least as much as which family — a group label is a weak predictor of performance, and the representative chosen inside the family carries most of the signal. sections.heading: VI-D Is the Ordering Real?
sections.text: A ranking of 64 single runs invites the obvious objection that it is noise. We separate two sources of that noise and can address only one of them honestly. Evaluation uncertainty — would a different test split reorder the table? — we can measure. The independent unit here is the scene , not the frame: the 240 test frames are 5 scenes seen from 48 viewpoints each, and views of one tree are not independent samples. We therefore cluster-bootstrap the 5 test scenes (2000 resamples) and re-rank every encoder on each resample. The ordering is stable: the re-ranked order correlates with the reported one at Spearman ρ = 0.994 \rho=0.994{} (2.5th percentile 0.962), and internimage_t is first in 100% of resamples. The reason the paired comparison is far tighter than the marginal error bars would suggest is that every encoder is scored on the identical frames, so scene difficulty is a common term that cancels between encoders even though it dominates each encoder’s absolute score. Training uncertainty — would a different seed reorder the table? — we cannot measure, because each encoder was trained once. 64 encoders at multiple seeds was beyond the compute available, and this is the sharpest limitation of the study: the analysis above bounds the noise from which trees we tested on , not from how the run happened to go . Differences of a few thousandths in Table I should not be read as ordering evidence; the effects we build conclusions on — the collapse of 25 encoders, the gap between the top and bottom of the ranking, and the seg–depth correlation — are all far larger than that.

sections.heading: VI-E Do the Two Tasks Prefer the Same Encoder?
sections.text: A shared encoder is only justified if segmentation and depth want the same features. They do. Ranking the 64 encoders by segmentation and by depth gives a Spearman rank correlation of ρ = 0.89 \rho=0.89{} (Fig. 4 ): an encoder that is good for one task is almost always good for the other. The practical consequence is that the shared-trunk design costs almost nothing in this setting — there is no meaningful subset of encoders that trades segmentation for depth — and that a single backbone recommendation serves both heads. Fig. 4 : Rank on segmentation (mIoU) against rank on depth ( δ 1 \delta_{1} ). Points cluster on the diagonal (top-left is best on both), giving a strong Spearman correlation and showing that the two tasks prefer the same encoders.

sections.heading: VI-F Qualitative Behaviour
sections.text: Fig. 5 : Qualitative segmentation on three held-out test scenes. Columns: left image, ground-truth tree mask, the best encoder (internimage_t) and a degenerate one (resnext50_16x4d); the two prediction columns are coloured against the ground truth. The per-panel tree IoUs are within a few points of each other, so region IoU cannot separate the columns — but resnext50_16x4d has answered “tree” almost everywhere and floods every gap in the canopy with false positives (red), while internimage_t keeps the background between the branches open. Boundary F1, in the column headers, separates them at once. Fig. 6 : Qualitative depth on the same three scenes. Columns: left image, ground-truth depth, the best encoder (internimage_t), and the lowest-ranked encoder overall (resmlp_12). The strong encoder recovers the fine branch structure and tracks the ground truth; the weakest produces horizontally-streaked depth unrelated to the scene. Depth is drawn on each model’s own predicted tree mask, which is why a segmentation failure is visible here as well. The metric argument of Section IV is not hypothetical: it is visible in the predictions themselves (Fig. 5 ). resnext50_16x4d — a 12.9 M classical residual network, precisely the kind of backbone a project inherits on reputation — reaches 0.929 tree IoU against 0.943 for the best encoder, and on that number alone would pass for competent. Its background IoU is 0.012 and its boundary F1 is 0.000: it has learned to answer “tree” and nothing else, and the silhouette the cutter needs is simply absent. internimage_t, at 0.357 background IoU and 0.419 BF1, holds the gaps between the branches open instead. With 25 of 64 encoders in this state, the failure is the common case rather than a curiosity. The same encoder-driven gap appears in depth (Fig. 6 ). internimage_t tracks ground-truth depth closely and keeps thin twigs separated from the background behind them, whereas resmlp_12, last of the 64 by composite score (0.032 δ 1 \delta_{1} , 44.64 px EPE), produces depth that bears little relation to the scene. Because depth is consumed on the predicted tree mask, a segmentation failure propagates straight into the depth a downstream controller would act on — which is why the boundary and background terms, rather than the near-saturated region IoU, drive the ranking.

sections.heading: VII Discussion
sections.text: How much does the encoder decide? A great deal. Even after removing the 25 collapsed models, the 39 that remain span 0.314–0.654 mIoU and 0.032–0.725 depth δ 1 \delta_{1} — a factor of two on segmentation and effectively the whole usable range on depth, from a change of encoder alone. The encoder is not a free choice that a downstream head can compensate for; it sets the ceiling. From-scratch training reshapes the ranking. The clearest single effect is that data-hungry plain transformers collapse without pretraining — 3 of 4 — which is why group E sits at the bottom despite two of its members being the largest models in the study. This is a property of the training regime we chose in order to isolate architecture, and it is the main reason our ordering should not be read as a universal backbone ranking (see limitations). Architecture beats parameters. The Pareto front is populated by compact convolutional and hybrid encoders, and the largest models are dominated. On thin-structure segmentation and depth, the inductive bias of the architecture matters more than raw capacity — the opposite of what a parameter-count heuristic would suggest. One backbone is enough. The strong seg–depth rank correlation means the shared-encoder assumption is well founded here: there is no genuine trade-off to manage, so a single recommendation — a compact modern or classical convolutional encoder — serves both heads at once.

sections.heading: VIII Limitations
sections.text: Four limitations bound what these numbers support, in roughly decreasing order of how much they should worry a reader. Single seed. Every encoder was trained once. Section VI-D bounds the noise from the choice of test scenes but says nothing about run-to-run variance, so small differences in Table I carry no weight; only the large effects should be read as findings. Synthetic data, and only 5 test scenes. All conclusions are on rendered forest scenes. Exact geometric labels are what make thin-structure evaluation possible at all — no hand annotation resolves a two-pixel twig — but rendered canopies lack the sensor noise, motion blur and illumination of field imagery, and transfer is untested here. The test split is also narrow: 5 trees. No pretraining. Training from scratch isolates architecture but removes an advantage that some families, plain transformers in particular, benefit from more than others. Our ordering should be read as a from-scratch ordering, not a universal backbone ranking; establishing whether pretraining reorders it is the obvious next experiment. One representative per family, unequal budgets. Within-family variance is not measured and a different preset could move a family. Four families are represented only at ∼ \sim 100 M because they publish nothing smaller, though their weak results cut against capacity rather than for it. 64 encoders completed; the remainder exceeded the memory budget or had not finished.

sections.heading: IX Conclusion
sections.text: We asked how much the encoder decides on joint tree segmentation and stereo depth, and answered it by swapping only the encoder — 64 of them, one per architecture family, trained from scratch — through a fixed segmentation branch, a fixed stereo branch and an evaluation built to resist the label-everything-tree shortcut. The encoder decides a great deal: compact convolutional and hybrid backbones lead (internimage_t best overall), 3 of 4 plain transformers collapse without pretraining, parameter count fails to predict quality, and segmentation and depth agree strongly enough ( ρ = 0.89 \rho=0.89{} ) that one shared backbone serves both. For thin-structure perception in forestry robotics, the practical recommendation is to choose a compact modern or classical convolutional encoder by measurement on the target task rather than by inheriting whichever backbone is strong on ImageNet.

sections.heading: Reproducibility and Availability
sections.text: The sweep is one resumable command that trains and evaluates each encoder in an isolated subprocess and records per-encoder failures rather than aborting. Every table, figure and in-text number above — including the bootstrap of Section VI-D and the masks in Fig. 5 , which are recovered from the stored predictions and checked against each run’s own per-frame record — is emitted from the result files by a single script; nothing is transcribed by hand. Code, the tree50 renderer and the trained checkpoints will be released with the paper.

A Controlled Comparison of 64 Vision Backbones on Joint Tree Segmentation and Stereo Depth Yida Lin, Bing Xue, Mengjie Zhang Affiliation: Centre for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Victoria University of Wellington, Wellington, New Zealand linyida @ myvuw.ac.nz, bing.xue @ vuw.ac.nz, mengjie.zhang @ vuw.ac.nz Sam Schofield, Richard Green Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Software Engineering University of Canterbury, Canterbury, New Zealand sam.schofield @ canterbury.ac.nz, richard.green @ canterbury.ac.nz Abstract A robot that prunes trees needs two facts about the same pixel: whether it belongs to a tree, and how far away it is. Both are normally obtained by attaching a task head to a vision backbone, and the backbone is chosen by reputation rather than by measurement. We ask a narrow but answerable question: with the dataset, the decoders, the losses, the schedule and the evaluation all held fixed, how much does the choice of encoder actually change joint semantic segmentation and stereo depth on thin vegetation? We build a hard parameter-sharing network in which one shared encoder feeds a segmentation branch and a stereo branch, and in which only the encoder is swapped — a one-string change that retunes nothing downstream. We evaluate 64 encoders, one canonical representative per architecture family across 8 groups (classical, lightweight and modern CNNs, plain and hierarchical transformers, hybrids, MLP-mixers and state-space models), each at the preset nearest a common ∼ \sim 25 M budget and trained from scratch so that a pretrained checkpoint is not the confound; where a family publishes nothing near that budget, capacity is analysed explicitly rather than assumed away. Evaluation is deliberately unforgiving: depth is scored on tree pixels only, and segmentation is scored with boundary F1 and background IoU that a “label-everything-tree” collapse cannot win. Three findings stand out. First, the strongest encoders are convolutional and hybrid, not transformer: internimage_t leads with 0.650 segmentation mIoU and 0.725 depth δ 1 \delta_{1} , while 3 of the 4 plain vision transformers collapse when trained from scratch. Second, parameters do not predict quality — edgenext_xxs, at only 1.2 M encoder parameters, outranks models nearly two orders of magnitude larger. Third, the segmentation and depth rankings agree strongly (Spearman ρ = 0.89 \rho=0.89{} ), so the shared encoder faces no genuine task conflict and a single backbone serves both. Along the way, 25 of 64 encoders collapse to a degenerate all-tree segmentation that region IoU hides but boundary F1 exposes — a reminder that the metric, not only the backbone, decides what a comparison can see. Index Terms: encoder comparison, multi-task learning, hard parameter sharing, semantic segmentation, stereo depth estimation, vision backbones, thin structures, forestry robotics I Introduction A robot that prunes trees must answer two questions about the same pixel. The first is one of membership: is this pixel part of a tree, or part of the background behind it? The second is one of geometry: how far away is it? Neither answer is useful alone. Perfect segmentation without depth cannot guide a cutter; perfect depth without a tree mask cannot tell the cutter where the wood is. Both tasks are, in practice, built the same way: take a vision backbone, attach a decoder, and train. The backbone holds most of the parameters and most of the compute, and it is usually chosen by reputation — whatever performed well on ImageNet classification, or whatever the previous paper in the area used. That inheritance is rarely questioned, and it is not obviously safe. Tree canopies are not ImageNet: the objects are thin, self-occluding, repetitive and semi-transparent, and the discriminative signal lives in high-frequency boundaries rather than in object-level texture. This paper asks a deliberately narrow question, because the narrow version is the one that can be answered: with everything else held fixed, how much does the encoder decide? We are not proposing a new architecture. We are measuring how much the architecture choice is worth on a task whose conventional wisdom was formed somewhere else. Answering it requires a setup in which the encoder is genuinely the only thing that changes, and an evaluation that cannot be won by a shortcut: trees fill 75–91% of every tree50 frame, so region IoU is nearly saturated before a model has learned anything. We therefore score depth on tree pixels only and segmentation with boundary F1 and background IoU, which a “label-everything-tree” collapse cannot win. Our contributions are: • A two-task benchmark in which the encoder is the only free variable. A hard parameter-sharing network feeds one shared encoder into a segmentation branch and a stereo branch. Every encoder exposes the same five-scale feature contract, so swapping it is a one-string change; the decoders, losses, schedule and evaluation never move. • 64 encoders, one per family, from scratch. One canonical representative per architecture family across 8 groups, taken at the preset nearest a common budget with ablation-only variants excluded, and trained without pretrained weights so that a checkpoint is not the confound. Where families publish nothing near that budget, capacity is measured rather than assumed away. • An evaluation designed to resist the obvious cheat. Depth on tree pixels only; segmentation reported with boundary F1 and background IoU alongside region IoU, so a degenerate all-tree solution is visible rather than rewarded. • A measured answer. Convolutional and hybrid encoders lead while most plain transformers collapse from scratch; parameter count does not predict quality; and the segmentation and depth orderings are strongly correlated, so one shared backbone suffices for both tasks. II Related Work II-A Perception for Tree and Orchard Robotics Robots that work on woody plants — harvesting, thinning, pruning, forwarding — have converged on the same perception requirement: a per-pixel decision about what is plant and where it is in space [ 28 , 29 ] . Field pruning systems report that perception, not manipulation, is the binding constraint [ 30 ] , and the first autonomous forestry machines make the same observation at a larger scale [ 31 ] . What these systems need from a network is exactly the pair we study: a tree mask that follows the true silhouette, and a depth estimate on the pixels inside it. Two properties of the domain make it a poor match for the assumptions behind ImageNet-era backbone design. First, the targets are thin : branches and twigs are a few pixels wide, so the signal lives in high-frequency boundaries rather than object-level texture — the same difficulty that motivated dedicated treatment of wires and cables in aerial robotics [ 32 ] . Second, exact labels on thin structures are effectively unobtainable by hand, which is why rendered data has become a standard instrument for agricultural segmentation [ 33 ] and is what we use here. What is missing from this literature is a controlled measurement of how much the backbone contributes, which is the gap this paper addresses. II-B Vision Backbones The encoder families we compare correspond to the main lines of backbone research. Classical convolutional networks established depth, residual connections and cardinality as the levers of representational power [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Efficiency-driven designs traded dense convolution for depthwise-separable and shuffled operations to reach mobile budgets [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Vision transformers replaced the inductive bias of convolution with global attention [ 8 , 9 ] , and hierarchical variants reintroduced locality and multi-scale structure to make attention affordable for dense prediction [ 10 , 11 ] . Modern convolutional networks then showed that much of the transformer advantage could be recovered by convolutional designs with large kernels and modernised training recipes [ 12 , 13 ] . Hybrids interleave the two families [ 14 , 15 ] , attention-free MLP designs question whether attention is required at all [ 16 , 17 ] , and state-space models offer linear-complexity sequence mixing as a third alternative [ 18 , 19 ] . These families are usually compared on ImageNet classification, occasionally on COCO detection or ADE20K segmentation. We are not aware of a controlled comparison on a task that couples dense semantic segmentation with stereo geometry on thin structures, which is the regime this paper targets. II-C Multi-Task Learning Sharing one encoder between related tasks is the standard way to amortise computation, and hard parameter sharing — one shared trunk, independent task-specific heads — remains the reference formulation [ 20 , 21 ] . Richer schemes add cross-task connections, cascades or attention between branches [ 22 , 23 ] . We deliberately use the plain hard-sharing form: any cross-task pathway would give the encoder a second route to influence the result and would blur exactly the attribution this paper is trying to make. II-D Stereo Matching and Segmentation Our stereo branch follows the cost-volume lineage: features are correlated across a disparity range, aggregated with 3D convolutions, and reduced by soft-argmin [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] . The segmentation branch is a standard U-Net encoder–decoder [ 27 ] that fuses the five encoder scales into a per-pixel tree/background labelling. Both branches are held fixed across all 64 encoders; the only thing that changes between runs is the shared trunk that feeds them. III Benchmark Design III-A Data We use the tree50 corpus: 50 rendered forest scenes, each captured from 48 viewpoints, giving 2,400 rectified stereo pairs at 1920 × 1080 1920\times 1080 with per-pixel depth and tree masks. Splits are scene-exclusive — scenes 1–40 train, 41–45 validate, 46–50 test — so no tree is ever seen from a different angle at test time. Because the renderer exports geometry rather than hand annotation, the labels are exact on precisely the thin structures that manual labelling cannot reach. We state the size of the test set in the units that matter: it is 240 frames but only 5 independent scenes , since the 48 views of one scene show the same trees. Everything reported below is therefore an average over 5 trees, and Section VI-D quantifies what that costs in confidence. Two measured properties of the data shaped the design, and each is enforced by an assertion in the codebase rather than left as a convention. First, disparity is an exact function of depth, d = f x ​ B / z d=f_{x}B/z , agreeing with the rendered output to 0.0 0.0 px on average; depth and disparity are therefore the same signal in two units, so the network predicts disparity once and converts. Second, trees occupy 75–91% of the pixels. This is why region IoU is a weak metric here and why depth is scored on tree pixels only (Section IV ). One encoder, applied to both views with shared weights, produces five feature scales; a segmentation branch and a stereo branch consume them independently, with no connection between the branches. Only the encoder is swapped — everything to the right of f 0 ​ … ​ f 4 f_{0}\ldots f_{4} is identical across all 64 runs. The left and right images pass through the same encoder weights, producing five feature maps at strides 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 2,4,8,16,32 (Fig. 1 ). The segmentation branch is a U-Net decoder over all five scales, emitting a per-pixel tree/background labelling. The stereo branch builds a group-wise correlation cost volume from the left and right stride-4 features, aggregates it with 3D convolutions, reduces it by soft-argmin, and refines the result residually; depth follows from disparity by z = f x ​ B / d z=f_{x}B/d . Beyond the shared encoder there is no connection between the branches. 1 1 1 The segmentation decoder also carries centre and offset heads for an instance-grouping extension outside the scope of this paper. They are neither analysed nor reported, but they are present and supervised in every run, so they shift the absolute numbers for all encoders alike rather than favouring any one of them. III-C The Five-Scale Contract The comparison is only meaningful if the encoder is genuinely interchangeable. Every encoder implements one method, forward_features , returning five maps whose i i -th spatial size is exactly ⌈ H / 2 i + 1 ⌉ \lceil H/2^{i+1}\rceil . The contract fixes ratios , not sizes, so the same encoder serves any input resolution; only the channel counts differ. Inputs are reflection-padded to a multiple of 32 and each level is cropped back, so padding never leaks into the feature sizes. III-D Encoder Selection Two levels of organisation are used throughout and are not interchangeable. A family is one published architecture line (ResNeXt, Swin, ConvNeXt, …); a group is the broad design paradigm it belongs to, of which there are 8, labelled A–I. We select one representative per family , giving 64 encoders spread over the 8 groups. The selection applies three rules, in order. First, exclude ablation-only variants : several families ship control conditions alongside their proposal — a large-kernel network with the kernels reduced to 3 × 3 3\times 3 , a state-space model with the state-space mixing removed — and representing a family by its own control would understate it. Second, target the parameter budget : among the remainder we take the preset closest to a common ∼ \sim 25 M encoder budget, the tier at which most families publish their reference model. Third, prefer canonical naming when the first two rules tie. A small hand-curated override fixes the cases where the automatic rule still picks a non-canonical variant. We state plainly that this targets a budget rather than matching one. Families do not publish on a common grid: only 22 of 64 encoders (34%) land within ± \pm 10 M of the target, the median is 11.7 M, and the range is 0.2–100.3 M — four families whose smallest published variant is a ∼ \sim 100 M base model are represented at that size. Rather than discard the families that do not fit, we keep them and treat capacity as a measured covariate: Fig. 3 plots quality directly against encoder size, and the result — that the largest models are among the worst — is what licenses reading the rest of the comparison as being about architecture rather than about scale. IV Evaluation Protocol All metrics are computed on the left image of the test split. IV-A Segmentation We report tree-versus-background mean IoU (mIoU), the individual background and tree IoUs, boundary F1 at a 2 px tolerance (BF1), and pixel accuracy. The metric we consider most diagnostic is not region IoU but boundary F1 together with background IoU . Because trees fill most of the frame, a model that simply labels every pixel “tree” already scores ∼ \sim 0.93 tree IoU while contributing nothing: its background IoU is near zero and its boundary F1 collapses. Region IoU hides this failure; the boundary and background terms expose it. Since the downstream task needs the tree silhouette , the boundary term is the one that matters. IV-B Depth Depth is evaluated on ground-truth tree pixels only . Sky and ground are geometrically trivial and would dilute the metric with the easy majority. We report AbsRel, RMSE, SILog and δ < 1.25 k \delta<1.25^{k} , plus disparity EPE and bad- τ \tau rates on the same pixel set. One property of this pixel set deserves stating, because it makes the mean error look worse than the prediction is. Tree pixels include distant twigs at the far end of the disparity range, where a sub-pixel disparity error maps to a metric depth error of several metres. The absolute error is therefore strongly right-skewed, and mean-based scores are set by that tail rather than by the typical pixel: the best encoder has 0.786 AbsRel and 1.39 m mean absolute error, but a median absolute error of 0.20 m, with 2.45 m at the 90th percentile. We report the mean-based metrics because they are the convention and keep this work comparable, but read them as tail statistics; the median and the percentiles describe what a controller would see on most of the branch it is actually reaching for. Two secondary views are reported because they answer questions the primary one hides: per-tree averaging weights each tree equally rather than each pixel, so a model that has learned only the large foreground tree separates from one that also handles the distant small ones; and depth restricted to the predicted tree mask measures end-to-end usability, since a segmentation error propagates into the depth that is actually consumed. IV-C Efficiency We report end-to-end FPS, peak memory, encoder parameters and GFLOPs, measured on the whole two-branch network. Since the decoders are byte-identical across runs, differences between rows are attributable to the encoder even though the figures themselves are whole-system costs. V Experimental Setup All encoders are trained from scratch — no pretrained weights — so that the comparison measures architecture rather than the availability and quality of a checkpoint. This lowers absolute accuracy and is a deliberate trade; it also means the ranking here need not match one obtained with pretrained initialisation, a point we return to in the limitations. Every encoder receives an identical schedule: AdamW at learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 2 10^{-2} , cosine decay after linear warmup, mixed precision, gradient clipping at norm 1.0 1.0 , and 100 epochs at 512 × 288 512\times 288 with batch size 12. Normalisation layers and biases are excluded from weight decay. The checkpoint is selected by lowest total validation loss rather than by any single task metric, since selecting on one metric would quietly turn the run into single-task model selection. The segmentation branch is supervised by cross-entropy and the stereo branch by smooth- L 1 L_{1} on disparity at both the coarse and refined stages. The cost volume is built at stride 4 over a disparity range that covers the native maximum, and the segmentation decoder uses channel widths ( 128 , 96 , 64 , 48 ) (128,96,64,48) . Every resolution-dependent constant — chiefly the disparity search range and the boundary-F1 tolerance — is defined once at native resolution and derived for any other resolution by a single function, so that supervision and evaluation cannot silently disagree. Encoders are trained in isolated subprocesses so that a memory failure in one cannot corrupt the allocator state of the next. Where an encoder does not fit at the nominal batch size, the micro-batch is reduced and gradient accumulation is raised to hold the effective batch constant; holding the effective batch fixed matters because batch size changes normalisation statistics and gradient noise, and an encoder penalised for a memory property rather than for its representational quality would defeat the purpose of the comparison. State-space and global-attention encoders are the systematic pressure point here, since their activation memory far exceeds what their parameter count suggests; of the full selection, 64 encoders completed training and are reported below. VI-D Is the Ordering Real? A ranking of 64 single runs invites the obvious objection that it is noise. We separate two sources of that noise and can address only one of them honestly. Evaluation uncertainty — would a different test split reorder the table? — we can measure. The independent unit here is the scene , not the frame: the 240 test frames are 5 scenes seen from 48 viewpoints each, and views of one tree are not independent samples. We therefore cluster-bootstrap the 5 test scenes (2000 resamples) and re-rank every encoder on each resample. The ordering is stable: the re-ranked order correlates with the reported one at Spearman ρ = 0.994 \rho=0.994{} (2.5th percentile 0.962), and internimage_t is first in 100% of resamples. The reason the paired comparison is far tighter than the marginal error bars would suggest is that every encoder is scored on the identical frames, so scene difficulty is a common term that cancels between encoders even though it dominates each encoder’s absolute score. Training uncertainty — would a different seed reorder the table? — we cannot measure, because each encoder was trained once. 64 encoders at multiple seeds was beyond the compute available, and this is the sharpest limitation of the study: the analysis above bounds the noise from which trees we tested on , not from how the run happened to go . Differences of a few thousandths in Table I should not be read as ordering evidence; the effects we build conclusions on — the collapse of 25 encoders, the gap between the top and bottom of the ranking, and the seg–depth correlation — are all far larger than that. VI-E Do the Two Tasks Prefer the Same Encoder? A shared encoder is only justified if segmentation and depth want the same features. They do. Ranking the 64 encoders by segmentation and by depth gives a Spearman rank correlation of ρ = 0.89 \rho=0.89{} (Fig. 4 ): an encoder that is good for one task is almost always good for the other. The practical consequence is that the shared-trunk design costs almost nothing in this setting — there is no meaningful subset of encoders that trades segmentation for depth — and that a single backbone recommendation serves both heads. VII Discussion How much does the encoder decide? A great deal. Even after removing the 25 collapsed models, the 39 that remain span 0.314–0.654 mIoU and 0.032–0.725 depth δ 1 \delta_{1} — a factor of two on segmentation and effectively the whole usable range on depth, from a change of encoder alone. The encoder is not a free choice that a downstream head can compensate for; it sets the ceiling. From-scratch training reshapes the ranking. The clearest single effect is that data-hungry plain transformers collapse without pretraining — 3 of 4 — which is why group E sits at the bottom despite two of its members being the largest models in the study. This is a property of the training regime we chose in order to isolate architecture, and it is the main reason our ordering should not be read as a universal backbone ranking (see limitations). Architecture beats parameters. The Pareto front is populated by compact convolutional and hybrid encoders, and the largest models are dominated. On thin-structure segmentation and depth, the inductive bias of the architecture matters more than raw capacity — the opposite of what a parameter-count heuristic would suggest. One backbone is enough. The strong seg–depth rank correlation means the shared-encoder assumption is well founded here: there is no genuine trade-off to manage, so a single recommendation — a compact modern or classical convolutional encoder — serves both heads at once. VIII Limitations Four limitations bound what these numbers support, in roughly decreasing order of how much they should worry a reader. Single seed. Every encoder was trained once. Section VI-D bounds the noise from the choice of test scenes but says nothing about run-to-run variance, so small differences in Table I carry no weight; only the large effects should be read as findings. Synthetic data, and only 5 test scenes. All conclusions are on rendered forest scenes. Exact geometric labels are what make thin-structure evaluation possible at all — no hand annotation resolves a two-pixel twig — but rendered canopies lack the sensor noise, motion blur and illumination of field imagery, and transfer is untested here. The test split is also narrow: 5 trees. No pretraining. Training from scratch isolates architecture but removes an advantage that some families, plain transformers in particular, benefit from more than others. Our ordering should be read as a from-scratch ordering, not a universal backbone ranking; establishing whether pretraining reorders it is the obvious next experiment. One representative per family, unequal budgets. Within-family variance is not measured and a different preset could move a family. Four families are represented only at ∼ \sim 100 M because they publish nothing smaller, though their weak results cut against capacity rather than for it. 64 encoders completed; the remainder exceeded the memory budget or had not finished. IX Conclusion We asked how much the encoder decides on joint tree segmentation and stereo depth, and answered it by swapping only the encoder — 64 of them, one per architecture family, trained from scratch — through a fixed segmentation branch, a fixed stereo branch and an evaluation built to resist the label-everything-tree shortcut. The encoder decides a great deal: compact convolutional and hybrid backbones lead (internimage_t best overall), 3 of 4 plain transformers collapse without pretraining, parameter count fails to predict quality, and segmentation and depth agree strongly enough ( ρ = 0.89 \rho=0.89{} ) that one shared backbone serves both. For thin-structure perception in forestry robotics, the practical recommendation is to choose a compact modern or classical convolutional encoder by measurement on the target task rather than by inheriting whichever backbone is strong on ImageNet.
